analysis.one_liner: Requires refunds, with interest, of overcharges paid for electricity in Western states during the energy crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a California Democrat with 21 cosponsors, was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on August 16, 2001, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2000 and 2001, wholesale electricity prices in the West spiked during the California energy crisis. This bill would have ordered the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, within 30 days of enactment, to refund with interest every rate or charge from that period that exceeded a fair, cost-based rate, using pricing formulas tougher than the ones the commission had chosen on its own in June 2001. It would also have let any affected state sue in federal court to force the refunds.
analysis.who_benefits: Households, businesses, and utilities in Western states that paid inflated wholesale electricity prices between October 2000 and June 2001 would receive refunds plus interest. States would get a new tool to enforce the refunds in court.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds, with interest, of any rates and charges that exceeded just and reasonable rates for electricity sold in the Western region between October 2, 2000 and June 20, 2001, with the money going back to those who paid it [S3].

Requires the commission to calculate fair rates using cost-of-service formulas or a tightened version of its own June 19, 2001 order — removing a 10 percent creditworthiness adder and eliminating a premium above the mitigated market price — which would have produced larger refunds than the commission's existing formula [S3].
Lets any affected state enforce the refund order in federal district court, giving state governments a way to act if the commission did not [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers — the utilities and generating companies whose rates the commission found excessive — would pay the refunds plus interest.

drawbacks.text: Retroactively rewriting rates to cost-of-service levels could have discouraged generators and investors from building or selling power in Western markets, an objection the industry raised against tougher refund formulas during the crisis [S3].
The refunds would flow first to the utilities and large buyers that paid the inflated rates, so individual households would only benefit if those buyers passed the money back to customers [S3].

By dictating the commission's methodology in statute and letting states sue in federal court, the bill would have overridden FERC's own June 2001 settlement of the refund question and invited years of litigation over every price [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core purpose is straightforward consumer protection: money was paid above fair rates, and the bill returns it with interest. The honest costs are that retroactive rate-setting risks chilling investment in generation, and the enforcement design — statutory formulas plus state lawsuits — was more blunt than the commission's ongoing process. Those are real but secondary against a multibillion-dollar overcharge, and the bill's death meant none of the tradeoff was ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee in August 2001, and sat there until Congress ended in January 2003 without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jane Harman introduced the bill on August 2, 2001, and 21 House colleagues — all Democrats, almost all from California — joined as cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 16, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained with no further action for the rest of the 107th Congress [S5].

The bill targeted the period of the Western electricity crisis, October 2000 through June 2001, and was written to produce larger refunds than the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission had ordered on its own in June 2001 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers kept the charges they had collected above cost-based rates; no expanded refunds were ever ordered by this bill, and Western consumers never received the payments it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale electricity sellers kept the overcharges

for.name: Rep. Jane Harman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing FERC to refund Western electricity overcharges with interest, using tougher rate formulas than FERC's own June 2001 order [S1][S3].

for.name: 21 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 21 were Democrats, nearly all from California districts hit by the energy crisis [S4].

against.name: Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it was sent to a subcommittee in August 2001 and died there without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show opposition, but every one of its 22 sponsors was a House Democrat — 21 of 208 in that chamber — and no Republican ever cosponsored it [S4].

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers and merchant generators
industries.note: The bill would have forced companies that sold wholesale power during the 2000-2001 crisis to return charges above cost-based rates, plus interest. Their gain from the crisis was directly the public's loss, and the bill never passed, so they kept the money.

industries.industry: Investor-owned utilities in California and the West
industries.note: Utilities were the buyers who paid the inflated wholesale prices, and the refunds would go to those who paid. Their financial condition during the crisis was so damaged that one major California utility entered bankruptcy, and ratepayers ultimately shared the burden through higher retail rates.
